title: Tale of Hammad the Badawi

full_text:
In the vast red sands of the Najd lived Hammad, a Bedouin chief renowned across the desert for his skill with the lance, his generous hearth, and his unyielding adherence to the laws of nomadic honor. His tent was pitched beside an isolated desert crossroads, where a lantern burned all night on a tall pole to guide lost wayfarers.

One stormy night, when a violent sandstorm raged across the dunes, a lone horseman galloped up to Hammad’s tent, leaped from his exhausted mare, and begged for sanctuary according to the ancient laws of the desert. Hammad took the stranger's reins, ushered him into the tent, wrapped him in dry camel-hair cloaks, and slaughtered his prize young camel to prepare a hot feast.

As the guest sat before the hearth fire, the light illuminated his face. Hammad recognized him immediately: he was the chief of a rival clan who, in a border skirmish months before, had slain Hammad’s only brother! Hammad’s heart seized with grief and wrath, but he did not lay a finger upon his weapon or alter the warmth of his countenance.

For three days, Hammad served the guest with princely courtesy, pouring bitter coffee and serving roasted meat, according to the inviolable law that grants three days of unconditional protection to whoever breaks bread under one's tent. On the fourth morning, when the guest prepared to depart, Hammad led out the guest’s horse, fed and rested, and handed him a bag of dates and a full waterskin.

Hammad looked the rival chief in the eye and said quietly: 'Know, O guest, that you slew my brother in battle, and my heart bled every hour you sat at my hearth. But you sought my hospitality, and under Hammad’s roof, a guest is sacred. Today you leave my territory in peace. But if we meet tomorrow in the open desert, our blades must settle the score of our clans.'

The rival chief was so moved by such peerless chivalry and moral greatness that he threw down his sword, fell upon Hammad’s neck, and pledged eternal brotherhood between their tribes, ending forty years of desert warfare with a single act of sacred hospitality.
moral: Desert chivalry, hospitality to the stranger, and honoring the guest are sacred codes that triumph over enmity.

quiz.question: What is the central moral lesson taught in "Tale of Hammad the Badawi"?
options: Presence of mind and quiet wisdom triumph over brute strength.
Acting in haste and anger without thinking
Believing rumors and flattery without proof
